summary: This informational document discusses points to consider when designing a solution for identifying flows in MPLS networks. The key application is in-band performance monitoring of MPLS flows. It records considerations rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: To count how many cars use a road, you need to tell cars apart. This discusses ways to put labels on traffic so its speed can be measured.

questions: how to identify flows in mpls
what is mpls flow identification used for
how to measure packet loss in mpls
subtitle: What to weigh before designing a way to tell traffic flows apart inside an MPLS network.

tldr.problem: Operators want to measure packet loss and delay on real user traffic in MPLS networks, but packets in a flow are hard to tell apart from other traffic, especially with multiple sources and equal-cost multipath.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines no protocol. It lists considerations for any future flow identification design: loss and delay needs, units of identification, LSP types, scope, backwards compatibility, and data-plane and control-plane costs.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational set of design guidelines. Any solution should change the MPLS data plane as little as possible, stay optional and be disabled by default.

sections.title: Why Identify MPLS Flows
sections.content:
RFC 8372 discusses what to consider when developing a solution for MPLS flow identification. The key application is in-band performance monitoring of MPLS flows when MPLS encapsulates user data packets.

RFC 6374 defined loss and delay measurement for MPLS, but it relies on injected OAM packets to mark the start and end of a group of packets. Misordering of packets relative to those markers causes errors, and the method did not support different flow granularities or several ingress routers sending to one or more destinations.

Because loss is now very low in normal operation, active measurement with synthetic traffic is harder. Operators therefore need passive measurement of actual user traffic. The technique must be transparent to the end user, and no remnant of the measurement may leak into their network.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way was like counting cars by sending a special marker car down the road. Cars can overtake the marker and spoil the count, so people want to count the real cars instead.

sections.title: Loss and Delay Measurement Needs
sections.content:
Packet loss measurement is very sensitive to exactly which packets are being counted. Without some form of coloring or batch marking, as proposed in RFC 8321, accurate loss measurement of customer traffic may not be possible. So it may be necessary to mark packets so each one is assigned to a particular counter.

When traffic is subject to Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP), packets are grouped into batches so that the same batch can be counted at ingress and egress. Errors are especially large with ECMP because packets may cross different routers and different line cards, so transit times differ. If the label that identifies the batch changes, the chosen ECMP path does not change, whether the path is picked by deep packet inspection or by an entropy label (RFC 6790).

For delay, most existing methods are active and use injected test packets. Those packets may take different links from the real data under ECMP or link aggregation, so the delay of real traffic needs to be measured. A combined loss and delay measurement must satisfy both sets of considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: To count fairly, you must put cars into batches and count the same batch at both ends of the road. Cars may take different lanes, so the batches need clear tags.

sections.title: Units of Identification
sections.content:
The most basic unit is the identity of the node that handled the packet when it entered the MPLS network. The unit needed varies by use case, and identity may be needed at several layers of the label stack. The RFC considers four levels:

  • Per source LSR: everything from one source is aggregated.
  • Per group of LSPs: an ingress LSP aggregates a group, such as all the LSPs of a tunnel.
  • Per LSP: the basic form.
  • Per flow within an LSP: a fine-grained method.

Fine-grained identification may be possible by deep packet inspection, but not always, and doing it only at network entry and adding an identifier to the packet reduces work for other elements. The egress needs to identify the ingress LSR, a specific LSP, optionally an LSP group, and a flow within an LSP. How packets form a flow is specific to the application and out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: You could count all cars from one town, all cars on one road, or just one particular car. The more exact you want to be, the more you have to tag.

sections.title: LSP Types and Network Scope
sections.content:
For a point-to-point LSP (such as one made with RSVP-TE, or an MPLS Transport Profile LSP), the top label is unique to the ingress-egress pair at every hop. With Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP) disabled, the ingress LSR identity is available at the egress, so that part is regarded as a solved problem. Flow identity still needs more information in the packet or payload.

For a point-to-multipoint LSP without PHP, the ingress can also be inferred from the top label, but the flow may not be identifiable. A common solution for point-to-point and point-to-multipoint is desirable, and a context label (RFC 5331) is needed for the identity information.

In multipoint-to-point and multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs, the same label is normally used by multiple ingress LSRs, so the source cannot be found from the top label. Packets must explicitly convey the identity types. For multipoint-to-multipoint, the identity scope may be limited to LSPs ending at a common node.

Identification can be limited to flows uniquely identifiable at an ingress LSR, with no help from outside the MPLS domain. If identity is carried in the label stack, its scope stays within that MPLS domain, and the scope of a component of an LSP is limited to that LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: On a one-way private road you always know where a car came from. When many roads merge into one, cars arrive with no hint of where they began, so each one must carry a tag.

sections.title: Compatibility, Data Plane and Control Plane
sections.content:
Not all LSRs will support a new method, so a solution must be backwards compatible with deployed equipment and must not disable anything that works today. Identification must be an optional feature that is disabled by default. A solution may require all egress LSRs of a point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint LSP to support the identification type in use: either all are enabled or none.

MPLS users have set a very high bar for data-plane changes, so the method must minimize them. Methods needing no change should be preferred. A necessary change should be as small as possible and general purpose. Label stack size also matters, particularly for low-cost edge LSRs with limits on Label Stack Entries (LSEs), so a method must not consume too many labels or grow the stack too much.

The original 16 reserved labels need one LSE, and the special-purpose labels of RFC 7274 need two. Encoding flow identity with a special-purpose label therefore takes two LSEs, or three with the extended labels. Special-purpose labels are allowed, but other methods deserve careful consideration. On the control plane, a design should minimize complexity and the label coordination needed among LSRs.
sections.plainLanguage: Old equipment cannot be rebuilt, so new tags have to work alongside it and be switched off unless someone wants them. Tags that take lots of room on each package are a bad idea.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Adding originating or flow information to a packet gives more identity information and could weaken the privacy of the communication. Following the IETF concern about pervasive monitoring (RFC 7258), a solution should not degrade privacy below that of an MPLS network without the feature. The label is limited to the MPLS domain and does not depend on identifying the user data, which limits what can be observed.

A solution must not degrade the security of the MPLS network. Propagation of identification information outside the MPLS network that imposed it must be disabled by default, and the information should be restricted to the parts of the network that need it. For a fuller discussion, the RFC points to RFC 5920. There are no IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag that says who sent a package could reveal too much. So tags stay inside the network and are not handed outside by default.

items.text: Everything from one source is aggregated.

items.title: Per group of LSPs
items.text: An ingress LSP aggregates a group, such as all LSPs of a tunnel.
